title: Health Insurance Pricing
text:
The question
In one or two short paragraphs, introduce the setting, audience, focused research question, data source, observational unit, response, important predictors, and one important data limitation. Lead with what makes the question worth answering.
How is the amount spent on healthcare related to age, sex, BMI, number of children, smoking status, and region of the United States you life in? This study is for those setting health insurance pricing so that they can better understand the effect of these factors on the amount of health insurance a policyholder will need. Understanding these relationships can help insurance companies make more informed decisions when determining insurance premiums and help policyholders identify factors associated with higher healthcare costs. The data comes from the insurance.csv dataset, originally published in Brett Lantz’s Machine Learning with R and available through Kaggle. The observational unit is one individual, with a total of 1,338 individuals and seven variables. The response variable is charges, which represents the total annual healthcare charges for each individual. The six candidate predictors are age, sex, bmi, children, smoker, and region.
We expect smoking status to be one of the strongest predictors of healthcare charges, with age and BMI also likely to have important associations. Identifying these relationships may help insurance companies better understand healthcare costs when setting premiums and help policyholders recognize factors associated with higher insurance expenses. However, an important limitation is that the dataset is observational and provides limited information about its original data collection process. Therefore, we can identify associations between these variables and healthcare charges, but we cannot conclude that any of these factors directly cause healthcare costs to increase or decrease.

A new direction with AI

Show its substantive result on this page and summarize your independent checks. If the extension is an untaught comparator, evaluate it against the core course-based model. Link to the AI-use record instead of placing a transcript here.


Show code
# Implement the verified extension or show its most useful result.

library(tidymodels)

set.seed(502340)

folds <- vfold_cv(
  insurance_data,
  v = 10,
  repeats = 5
)

# Predictors to investigate
predictors <- c(
  "age",
  "sex",
  "bmi",
  "children",
  "smoker",
  "region"
)

# Number of random permutations
n_permutations <- 30

# Calculate permutation importance

importance_results <- map2_dfr(
  folds$splits,
  seq_along(folds$splits),

  function(split, i) {

    # Separate training and assessment observations
    train_data <- analysis(split)
    test_data <- assessment(split)

    # Fit regression using training observations
    model <- lm(
      charges ~ age + sex + bmi +
        children + smoker + region,
      data = train_data
    )

    # Original predictions and RMSE
    original_predictions <- predict(
      model,
      newdata = test_data
    )

    original_rmse <- rmse_vec(
      truth = test_data$charges,
      estimate = original_predictions
    )

    # Shuffle each predictor independently
    map_dfr(
      predictors,

      function(variable) {

        shuffled_rmse <- replicate(
          n_permutations,

          {
            shuffled_data <- test_data

            shuffled_data[[variable]] <-
              sample(shuffled_data[[variable]])

            predictions <- predict(
              model,
              newdata = shuffled_data
            )

            rmse_vec(
              truth = test_data$charges,
              estimate = predictions
            )
          }
        )

        tibble(
          fold = folds$id[i],
          repeat1 = folds$id2[i],
          variable = variable,
          original_rmse = original_rmse,
          permutation = seq_len(n_permutations),
          shuffled_rmse = shuffled_rmse,
          importance = shuffled_rmse - original_rmse
        )
      }
    )
  }
)


importance_summary <- importance_results %>%
  group_by(variable) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_importance = mean(importance),
    sd_importance = sd(importance),
    median_importance = median(importance),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_importance))

# check 1

first_split <- folds$splits[[1]]

train_check <- analysis(first_split)
test_check <- assessment(first_split)

check_model <- lm(
  charges ~ age + sex + bmi +
    children + smoker + region,
  data = train_check
)

check_predictions <- predict(
  check_model,
  newdata = test_check
)

# Method 1: yardstick
rmse_package <- rmse_vec(
  truth = test_check$charges,
  estimate = check_predictions
)

# Method 2: manual calculation
rmse_manual <- sqrt(
  mean(
    (test_check$charges -
       check_predictions)^2
  )
)
